title: How wine made the modern world
gist: A podcast interview with historian Kathleen Burk on her book 'Wine: A Global History' argues wine markets have always been made by political stability, shipping power and buyer taste rather than intrinsic quality — from Canaanite amphorae to the 1855 Bordeaux classification priced off English demand — and that climate change is now moving viticulture north while forcing Bordeaux to approve new grape varieties.

insights.claim: The earliest archaeological evidence of wine dates to around 8000 BC in the Caucasus, especially Georgia, and wine was discovered rather than invented.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Georgia's 10,000-year provenance claim is a durable marketing moat for an emerging wine-exporting region investors are only starting to notice.
insights.quote: The earliest evidence we have dates to about 8000 BC. Wine wasn’t invented – it was discovered.
insights.locator: What is the earliest archaeological evidence

insights.claim: Tartaric acid residue preserved inside excavated amphorae is the chemical fingerprint archaeologists use to identify ancient wine, making almost all pre-literate wine history dependent on residue analysis rather than texts.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Provenance and authenticity claims in fine wine increasingly rest on lab chemistry — the same toolkit now used to police counterfeit bottles.
insights.quote: They discovered tartaric acid preserved in the vessels, which became the fingerprint for identifying ancient wine.
insights.locator: Archaeologists painstakingly excavate sites

insights.claim: Domestication of the grape meant crossbreeding originally separate male and female vines into a hermaphroditic vine that fruits reliably without insect pollination, which is what made systematic winemaking possible.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The entire industry rests on a single ancient genetic bottleneck, which is precisely why climate-driven varietal substitution is so contentious.
insights.locator: Originally there were separate male and female grapevines

insights.claim: The Canaanites bundled amphorae of wine plus serving equipment — cup, ladle, strainer — with their cedar shipments to Egyptian pharaohs, creating demand for wine among rulers who then hired Canaanites as consultants to produce it themselves.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A 4,000-year-old template for razor-and-blade market entry: give the elite the full kit, then sell the know-how.
insights.locator: What role did the Canaanites and the Phoenicians play

insights.claim: Carthage, founded by the Phoenicians in what is now Tunisia, planted extensive vineyards and exported wine into Etruscan Italy before Greeks and then Romans supplanted the Phoenician trade.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: North Africa was a wine exporter long before Europe monopolised the category — relevant as Tunisia and Morocco rebuild quality wine industries.
insights.locator: One of their great achievements was founding Carthage

insights.claim: The Dutch dominated the wine trade for roughly three centuries because they held the world's largest merchant fleet, and they physically created modern Bordeaux by draining the marshland around it.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The most valuable terroir in the world is engineered land — a reminder that 'terroir' premia often originate in capital works, not nature.
insights.quote: They also made a remarkable contribution by draining marshland around Bordeaux. That transformed one of the world’s greatest wine-producing regions.
insights.locator: For one thing, the Dutch possessed the largest merchant fleet

insights.claim: Dutch merchants created the export markets for Loire Valley and Sauternes white wines by seeking supply for their own taverns, and smuggled French wine into Britain during the eighteenth-century Anglo-French wars.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Distributor demand, not producer ambition, has repeatedly created appellations — watch who controls the channel, not the vineyard.
insights.locator: The Dutch also wanted more white wine

themes.theme: Political stability as the precondition for viticulture

insights.claim: Mediterranean wine trade collapsed after Rome fell because piracy made sea transport dangerous, and the conquering peoples preferred beer and either neglected or destroyed vineyards.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Vineyards are a long-duration capital asset whose value is a direct function of secure trade routes — a live consideration for wine regions in unstable geographies.
insights.quote: Mediterranean wine trade declined dramatically because piracy made sea travel dangerous.
insights.locator: What happened to wine after Rome collapsed

insights.claim: Charlemagne's long period of relative peace, plus his encouragement of Rhine monasteries that needed wine for liturgy and traveller hospitality, is what revived European viticulture and pushed it into Germany and eventually Poland.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Institutional demand — liturgical, military, hospitality — has historically been the anchor tenant that lets a wine region get planted at all.
insights.locator: Things changed under Charlemagne

insights.claim: Within a generation of their foundation there were roughly 400 Cistercian monasteries, and monastic communities along pilgrimage routes turned wine into a thriving commercial enterprise by supplying pilgrims and Crusaders who believed wine gave strength and was safer than water.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Religious networks were the original scaled distribution system for wine, a precedent for how ideology can bootstrap a consumer category.
insights.locator: Monasteries were already widespread across Europe

insights.claim: Almost all wine was sweet until roughly the seventeenth century, because sugar was scarce apart from honey and residual sugar also acted as a preservative that extended shelf life after opening.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Consumer sweetness preference is a function of substitute availability, not innate taste — a framework transferable to today's low- and no-sugar beverage shifts.
insights.quote: Until about the seventeenth century, almost all wine was sweet.
insights.locator: What kind of wine were people drinking in the ancient world

insights.claim: For most people in the ancient and medieval world wine was not a luxury but basic sustenance: safer than water, calorie-dense and part of the everyday diet.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Wine's demand curve was staple-like for millennia; its repositioning as discretionary luxury is recent and therefore reversible in either direction.
insights.quote: It was safer than water, provided calories, and formed a basic part of the diet.
insights.locator: For most people, however, wine wasn’t simply a luxury

insights.claim: Ancient wine was strong enough that Greeks diluted it as much as twenty parts water to one part wine, while Romans diluted far less at roughly three parts water to two parts wine.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of how different the historical product was — useful for anyone marketing 'ancient method' wines on authenticity claims.
insights.quote: The Greeks generally diluted it very heavily – sometimes as much as twenty parts water to one part wine – because the wine itself was extremely strong.
insights.locator: It would have been a dark red, very sweet

insights.claim: The shift to light, clear 'claret' came from England's control of Aquitaine and Gascony during the Hundred Years' War, meaning English taste for drier wine was shaped by what English-held territory happened to produce.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Style preferences that later became global standards were set by supply availability under political control, not by consumer discovery.
insights.locator: It was closely connected to England’s control of parts of Aquitaine

insights.claim: The 1855 Bordeaux classification was not based on quality but on market price, and those prices were largely determined by what English buyers were willing to pay.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The most enduring quality hierarchy in wine is a frozen 1855 price list — meaning fine-wine investment grades encode a 170-year-old demand snapshot, not current quality.
insights.quote: In the end, the classification wasn’t based directly on quality but on market price – and those prices were largely determined by what English buyers were willing to pay.
insights.locator: They originated in 1855

insights.claim: Bordeaux brokers deliberately kept consumers ignorant of exact origins so buyers would keep purchasing through merchants rather than directly from producers.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Deliberate opacity as channel defence — the same disintermediation fight now playing out in direct-to-consumer wine.
insights.quote: The Bordeaux brokers preferred that consumers didn’t know exactly where the wines came from because they wanted buyers to continue purchasing through merchants rather than directly from producers.
insights.locator: The Bordeaux brokers preferred

insights.claim: The 1855 Classification still governs collector and investor behaviour today, particularly among buyers in Britain, the United States and China.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Three demand centres set fine-wine prices; Chinese collector appetite is therefore a swing factor in the asset class.
insights.locator: Remarkably, the 1855 Classification is still influential today

insights.claim: Britain remains the gatekeeper market: producers worldwide bring wines to London first because success in the British market often leads to success elsewhere.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: For any new wine region or brand, UK critical acceptance is the highest-leverage marketing spend.
insights.quote: Wine producers from around the world still bring their wines to London, hoping to establish themselves there first. Success in the British market often leads to success elsewhere.
insights.locator: By this period, the English had developed a reputation

insights.claim: Wine demand is broadening away from traditional Bordeaux elites toward Georgia, Ukraine, Germany and Austria, with consumers now guided by trusted critics and medals from publications such as Decanter rather than by classification alone.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Attention and shelf space are migrating to peripheral regions; incumbent classified-growth pricing power depends on collectors, not drinkers.
insights.quote: People now explore wines from Georgia, Ukraine, Germany, Austria and many other regions rather than focusing solely on the traditional elite wines of Bordeaux.
insights.locator: People now explore wines from Georgia

insights.claim: Roughly two-fifths of Americans drink no alcohol at all and around 70 per cent drink no wine, despite every US state now producing wine and high-quality output from California, Idaho, Washington State and Oregon.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: The largest wine-producing economy is also structurally under-consuming — a persistent gap that caps domestic demand growth for US wineries.
insights.locator: You point out that around two-fifths of Americans

insights.claim: Prohibition from 1920 to 1933 nearly destroyed the American wine industry, especially in California, and its lasting effect was to shift American palates from dry wine to sweet.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: A single 13-year regulatory shock reset national taste for decades — the clearest historical case for how policy, not preference, sets category structure.
insights.quote: Prohibition, from 1920 to 1933, nearly destroyed the American wine industry, especially in California.
insights.locator: Historically, the United States has been a spirits-drinking nation

insights.claim: Prohibition's fruit-juice loophole let California growers ship grapes to Chicago and New York — sometimes as compressed bricks with a hidden yeast packet and warnings not to mix them — keeping home winemaking alive among Italian-American families.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Regulatory arbitrage sustains demand through bans; prohibition rarely kills a category, it just reroutes and degrades it.
insights.quote: Grapes were sometimes packed into bricks with a packet of yeast hidden inside.
insights.locator: One allowed people to produce fruit juice

themes.theme: Climate change redraws the wine map

insights.claim: Warming is pushing wine production north, with Norway, Sweden and even Denmark now hosting wineries while Germany produces far more red wine than it once did.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Nordic viticulture is a real, investable consequence of warming — land values and appellation rules in northern Europe are the tell.
insights.quote: As the climate continues to warm, wine production is moving north. Norway now has several impressive wineries, as do Sweden and even Denmark.
insights.locator: How do you think climate change will affect wine

insights.claim: Southern regions including Châteauneuf-du-Pape in the southern Rhône are already struggling even with heat-tolerant varieties, and Bordeaux is expected to be heavily affected.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Southern French vineyard assets carry unpriced climate risk that will show up in yields and varietal composition before it shows up in prices.
insights.locator: It depends very much on where you are

insights.claim: Bordeaux has approved additional grape varieties including Portugal's Touriga Nacional, which raises the question of how much future Bordeaux will resemble the Bordeaux buyers think they are purchasing.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Varietal drift is a direct threat to the brand equity underpinning classified-growth valuations and long-dated cellar holdings.
insights.quote: That raises an important question: if Bordeaux wines increasingly rely on different grapes, how much will they still resemble the Bordeaux wines we know today?
insights.locator: Climate change is also changing which grape varieties

insights.claim: Burgundy growers reacted with horror to alternative grape varieties and remain determined to preserve Pinot Noir, meaning fine-wine producers are choosing identity preservation over adaptation and are trying to hold back forces much larger than themselves.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Burgundy's refusal to adapt means falling supply reliability against fixed prestige demand — structurally bullish scarcity, structurally bearish agronomics.
insights.quote: They are experimenting with different techniques to adapt, but ultimately they’re trying to hold back forces much larger than themselves.
insights.locator: Burgundy has taken a different approach

insights.claim: Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria, which have improved wine quality in recent decades, face the hardest climate adaptation problem and will need careful decisions on vineyard siting and heat management.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: North African wine is the most climate-exposed emerging supply source; capital committed there needs an altitude or coastal siting thesis.
insights.locator: By contrast, countries such as Tunisia, Morocco and Algeria

insights.claim: Islamic prohibition of wine was never applied consistently — ordinary people were forbidden while many rulers continued drinking — and wine persisted as coded metaphor in poetry, which Burk likens to an early form of Soviet samizdat.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Elite exemption plus underground circulation is the standard shape of a prohibited-goods market — a pattern worth applying to any regulated consumption category.
insights.quote: I’ve sometimes thought of this as an early form of samizdat – the underground circulation of literature in the Soviet Union.
insights.locator: One aspect I find especially interesting

insights.claim: The Qur'an both discourages wine and assumes people drink it — instructing believers not to attend prayers after drinking, and promising rivers of wine in Paradise — a tension poets exploited by asking why what is permitted in Paradise should be forbidden on earth.
insights.speaker: Engelsberg Ideas
insights.so_what: Doctrinal ambiguity has historically left room for tolerated consumption, relevant to how Gulf alcohol liberalisation is being justified today.
insights.locator: What does the Qur’an actually say about drinking wine
